name: Architectural Threshold as Episodic Boundary — How Spatial Transitions Segment Experience and Structure Memory
short_description: Doorway effect: spatial transitions trigger hippocampal context updating and episodic boundary creation; boundary strength scales with number of simultaneous channel changes
structural_pattern: Walking through an architectural threshold — a doorway, vestibule, narthex, courtyard, corridor, or any spatial boundary — triggers hippocampal context updating: the brain's situation model is refreshed, working memory for the previous context is partially cleared, and a new episodic representation is initiated (Radvansky & Copeland, 2006). This is the 'doorway effect.' Event Segmentation Theory (Zacks et al., 2007) provides the general framework: the brain partitions continuous experience into discrete events at moments of maximal multi-modal prediction error. THREE BOUNDARY STRENGTHS: WEAK (door between similar rooms, minimal context update), MODERATE (2-3 channel changes — room size + light level, or material + acoustic change), STRONG (4+ simultaneous channel changes — dark narrow stone corridor → bright tall atrium changes spatial, luminance, acoustic, material, thermal, motor all at once). Memory paradox: boundaries disrupt working memory for preceding context but ENHANCE encoding of the transition itself.
higher_order_principle: Spatial boundaries as memory boundaries. Architecture does not merely contain experience — it STRUCTURES memory by creating episodic boundaries at thresholds. The designer controls the memorial structure of architectural experience by controlling when and how strongly context changes at spatial transitions. This connects SC3 (which handles the emotional trajectory of the promenade) to the memory dimension: the promenade is not only an affective sequence but an episodic sequence — a series of memory-chapters whose vividness and separability depend on threshold design.

weak.description: Door between similar rooms (same size, light, material, temperature)
weak.memory_effect: Doorway effect present but attenuated, memory relatively continuous

moderate.description: 2-3 channel changes (room size + light level, or material + acoustic change)
moderate.memory_effect: Previous context partially cleared; new context encoded as distinct episode

strong.description: 4+ simultaneous channel changes (spatial, luminance, acoustic, material, thermal, motor)
strong.memory_effect: Transition itself encoded as vivid, independently retrievable memory

memory_consequences.boundary_paradox: Event boundaries disrupt working memory for preceding context (doorway effect) but ENHANCE encoding of the transition itself
memory_consequences.strong_thresholds: Buildings remembered as sequences of vivid episodes (distinct chapters)
memory_consequences.no_thresholds: Buildings remembered as vague, undifferentiated impressions — or not remembered at all

causal_links.evidence_base: Zacks et al. (2007) show that event boundary detection depends on multi-modal prediction error magnitude. The doorway effect (Radvansky & Copeland, 2006; Radvansky et al., 2011) demonstrates the spatial instantiation. The multi-channel parameterization (how many modalities change simultaneously) is the architectural extension — not yet directly tested but strongly predicted by EST.

The doorway effect is robust and well-replicated. Walking through a doorway into a different context produces measurable forgetting of the previous room's contents. The hippocampal context-updating mechanism is well supported by fMRI evidence (Spiers & Maguire, 2007).

Event boundaries enhance encoding of the boundary event itself (Zacks et al., 2007). The paradox: boundaries disrupt memory for the PRECEDING context but enhance memory for the TRANSITION. Consistent with Bermudez's extraordinary architectural experience data.

A building with many strong thresholds produces a richly segmented memorial structure. A building with no thresholds produces an undifferentiated memorial blur. There should be a Goldilocks zone for threshold density. Parallels SC3's threshold-density Goldilocks. Not yet tested experimentally.

scope_conditions: Applies to any building where occupants move between spaces — nearly all buildings
Effect requires physical movement through the threshold; visual observation of a threshold (looking through a doorway) produces weaker effect

Virtual doorway effects have been demonstrated (Radvansky et al., 2011), but physical movement through real architectural thresholds is expected to produce stronger effects due to multi-modal engagement
The doorway effect is attenuated when the occupant maintains a strong goal representation across the boundary (goal-driven navigation overrides context updating)
moderators: Occupant goal strength: strong navigational goals attenuate the doorway effect; exploratory wandering maximizes it
Familiarity: repeated traversal habituates the episodic boundary; a familiar doorway produces a weaker boundary than a novel one
Cognitive load: high cognitive load may attenuate boundary detection (reduced attentional resources for context monitoring)
Architectural intentionality: designed thresholds (vestibules, narthexes, ceremonial entries) produce stronger boundaries than incidental transitions (fire doors, utility corridors)

interactions.nature: SC3 describes the multi-modal PE trajectory. TP2 adds the MEMORY dimension: each SC3 threshold is simultaneously an episodic boundary. The promenade is both an emotional and a memorial sequence.
T23 formalizes hippocampal context memory. TP2 applies T23 to architectural thresholds: spatial boundaries trigger the hippocampal context updating that T23 describes.
TP1 adds the motor channel to thresholds: crossing a threshold involves a motor transition (different floor, different spatial demand) that contributes to the multi-modal context change.
Strong thresholds (compression → expansion, dark → light) can reach the awe threshold when the multi-modal PE magnitude exceeds the Goldilocks zone and the occupant accommodates rather than rejects.
